key_facts: **Vasculitis** is classified by vessel size: **small** (palpable purpura), **medium** (nodules, livedo racemosa, ulcers), **large** (rarely skin).
Always ask: is it skin-limited or systemic? Check **urine dipstick and BP** in every patient.
Biopsy an early lesion (<48 h) with direct IF; deep biopsy for medium-vessel disease.
Screen: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, ANA, ANCA, complement, hepatitis B/C, HIV, cryoglobulins, immunoglobulins.
Same-day: unwell, renal involvement, haemoptysis, neuropathy, gut ischaemia, or child with possible meningococcal disease.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Vasculitis** is inflammation of blood-vessel walls causing damage (haemorrhage, ischaemia). The skin is involved in many systemic vasculitides, and can be the only organ affected (**single-organ cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis**, the commonest form seen in dermatology).

head: Category
Examples
rows: Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), **granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)**, eosinophilic GPA (EGPA)
Anti-GBM disease, **cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis**, **IgA vasculitis (HSP)**, **hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis (anti-C1q vasculitis)**
**Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis**, cutaneous arteritis (= cutaneous PAN)
**HCV-associated cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis**, **HBV-associated PAN**, **drug-associated** immune-complex/ANCA vasculitis, cancer-associated vasculitis

ul: **"Skin vasculitis is just a rash"**: it can be the first sign of kidney or lung disease.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Vasculitis is **inflammation of vessel walls**; the size of vessel decides what you see.

mech.t: Immune complexes in post-capillary venules: palpable purpura, wheals.
mech.caption: Small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophils and red-cell leakage.

mech.t: Arteries at the dermo-subcutaneous junction: nodules, livedo racemosa, ulcers, digital infarcts.
ANCA activate neutrophils against small–medium vessels (GPA, MPA, EGPA).
The same process in kidney, lung, nerve and gut causes organ damage.

ul: **Immune-complex deposition** (antigen from a drug, infection, autoantigen or tumour → complexes deposit in post-capillary venules → complement activation → neutrophil influx → **leukocytoclasis** (nuclear dust), fibrinoid necrosis, red-cell extravasation = purpura).
**ANCA-mediated** neutrophil activation (MPO/PR3).
**Cell-mediated/granulomatous** inflammation.
**Direct infection** of the vessel wall (septic vasculitis — meningococcus, gonococcus, endocarditis).

**Common causes of cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis:** idiopathic (~45–55%), **infection** (~15–20% — streptococcal URTI, hepatitis B/C, HIV, endocarditis), **drugs** (~10–20% — β-lactams, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, allopurinol, thiazides, propylthiouracil/hydralazine (ANCA), TNF inhibitors, levamisole-contaminated cocaine), **connective tissue disease** (~15–20% — SLE, RA, Sjögren's), **malignancy** (<5% — haematological especially).

sections.title: Clinical features

blocks.h: Clinical features & sites — lesion → vessel size

head: Vessel size
Skin lesions
rows: **Palpable purpura**, petechiae, **urticarial plaques lasting >24 h**, haemorrhagic vesicles/bullae, pustules, superficial ulcers, splinter haemorrhages
**Subcutaneous nodules**, **livedo racemosa**, **deep punched-out ulcers**, digital infarcts/gangrene, papulonecrotic lesions

blocks: **Distribution:** dependent areas — **lower legs, ankles, feet, buttocks**; under tight clothing; in bed-bound patients the back and buttocks. Symptoms: burning/stinging or pain more than itch. Look for **systemic symptoms** (fever, arthralgia, abdominal pain, haematuria, cough/haemoptysis, sinusitis, neuropathy).

ol: **Confirm it is purpura:** **non-blanching on diascopy** (press a glass slide). Is it *palpable* (inflammatory → vasculitis) or *flat* (petechiae/ecchymoses → platelet/coagulation or capillaritis)?

**Skin biopsy** — the most useful test: **H&E:** punch from a **fresh lesion 24–48 h old** (LCV, vessel size); **Direct immunofluorescence (DIF):** a second biopsy from a lesion **<24 h old** (or perilesional), sent in **Michel's medium/saline, not formalin**. IgA → IgA vasculitis; IgM/C3 → cryoglobulins/immune complex; lupus band → HUVS/SLE; For suspected medium-vessel disease (nodules, livedo, ulcers), take a **deep incisional or elliptical biopsy to subcutaneous fat**, from a nodule or the **white centre of livedo**. A 4 mm punch often misses it

**Baseline screen for cause and organ involvement:** **Urinalysis (dipstick for blood and protein — the key bedside test)**; urine ACR/PCR; urine microscopy (red-cell casts); **Blood pressure.**; **FBC** (platelets — exclude thrombocytopenia; eosinophilia — EGPA/drug), **U&E/eGFR**, LFTs, **CRP/ESR**, clotting; **Immunology:** ANA, ENA, dsDNA, **ANCA (MPO/PR3)**, **C3/C4** (± C1q, anti-C1q), rheumatoid factor, **cryoglobulins** (sample kept at **37 °C** in transport), IgA level; **Infection:** **hepatitis B and C**, HIV, ASO/anti-DNase B, throat swab, **blood cultures** (endocarditis), ± IGRA (before immunosuppression); **Paraprotein:** serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, serum free light chains; As indicated: **CXR**, ECG/echo, faecal occult blood/calprotectin, CT angiography (PAN), nerve conduction studies
**Severity assessment:** BVAS (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score) in specialist care; Five-Factor Score for PAN/ANCA (see *Polyarteritis nodosa — systemic, HBV-associated and cutaneous*).

ul: **Non-vasculitic purpura:** thrombocytopenia (ITP, leukaemia, drugs), coagulopathy/anticoagulants, **DIC/meningococcal sepsis**, senile/actinic and **steroid purpura**, scurvy (perifollicular), capillaritis (pigmented purpuric dermatoses), trauma/non-accidental injury in children, raised intrathoracic pressure (petechiae above the nipple line after vomiting/coughing).

**Vasculopathies/occlusion (non-inflammatory):** antiphospholipid syndrome, cholesterol emboli, calciphylaxis, livedoid vasculopathy, warfarin necrosis, cryoglobulin/cryofibrinogen occlusion, septic emboli.
Also: pigmented purpuric dermatoses, stasis dermatitis, erythema multiforme/urticaria (blanching).

sections.title: Management

ul: **Treat the cause:** stop a suspected drug (record + Yellow Card); treat infection.

**Skin-limited, mild disease:** rest, **leg elevation**, **compression hosiery** if arterial supply is adequate, emollient, potent TCS for symptoms, antihistamine; NSAIDs only if not the culprit and renal function is normal. Most self-limiting episodes resolve in **3–4 weeks**.

**Chronic/recurrent skin-limited disease (specialist):** colchicine, **dapsone** (G6PD check; FBC/methaemoglobin monitoring), hydroxychloroquine; short prednisolone courses for necrotic/ulcerated disease; azathioprine/methotrexate/MMF for steroid-sparing.
**Systemic vasculitis:** specialist (rheumatology/renal) — glucocorticoids + cyclophosphamide/rituximab (ANCA), etc.
**Monitoring:** clinical (old lesions healing, new crops) + ESR/CRP; **urinalysis and BP** at each review — renal involvement can appear weeks later.

blocks: Recognition, urinalysis/BP, first-line bloods, stopping culprit drugs, symptomatic care and correct-urgency referral are within IP scope. Biopsy, immunosuppression and dapsone/colchicine regimens are specialist-led (shared care at most).

ul: **Lesions suggesting vasculitis:** palpable purpura, petechiae, urticarial plaques lasting >24 h, haemorrhagic vesicles/bullae, pustules, necrosis/ulcers, nodules, livedo racemosa, digital infarcts, splinter haemorrhages (see *Approach to cutaneous vasculitis*).

**How to diagnose:** clinical suspicion → **biopsy (H&E 24–48 h lesion + DIF <24 h; deep incisional for medium vessels)** → screen for cause and organ involvement (urinalysis, BP, FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, ANA/ENA/dsDNA, ANCA, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, RF, hepatitis B/C, HIV, ASO, SPEP, blood cultures, CXR) (see *Approach to cutaneous vasculitis*).

**Osler/Janeway:** Osler = tender immunological finger-pad nodules; Janeway = painless septic-embolic palm/sole macules. **Not pathognomonic** (SLE, gonococcaemia, typhoid, haemolytic anaemia, marantic endocarditis). **Splinters:** commonly traumatic/psoriatic; no validated threshold — new, multiple, proximal or multi-nail splinters plus fever/murmur raise concern (see *Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages*).

**Diagnosis:** **hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis (HUVS / anti-C1q vasculitis)**, with **lupus overlap** to exclude (ANA+, photosensitivity, arthralgia, low C3/C4, renal impairment): Strictly, Schwartz criteria require **≥6 months** of urticaria; she has had 3 months. Label it "hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis, probable HUVS"; The **creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL (~203 µmol/L)** indicates renal involvement → urgent nephrology

**Confirmatory tests:** skin biopsy with **DIF** (immunoreactants around vessels ± lupus band); **C1q level and anti-C1q antibodies**; CH50; **dsDNA, ENA**, antiphospholipid antibodies; **urinalysis, uPCR, urine microscopy ± renal biopsy**; cryoglobulins; hepatitis B/C; SPEP; CXR/PFTs; ophthalmology review (see *Urticarial vasculitis and hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome*).
**Task 1:** UV vs urticaria table; investigations (see *Urticarial vasculitis and hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome*).
**3a:** symmetrical non-blanching **palpable purpuric papules** (some confluent/haemorrhagic) on the lower legs.
**3b:** **cutaneous leukocytoclastic (small-vessel) vasculitis, drug-induced (NSAID)**.
**3c:** hydrostatic pressure, venous stasis and slow flow in dependent venules → immune-complex deposition (hence rest/elevation/hosiery).
**3d:** see *Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis*.
**3e:** **urinalysis**.
**3f:** see *Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis*.

**3g:** stop the NSAID, alternative analgesia, rest/elevation/compression, potent TCS/antihistamine; dapsone/colchicine/short prednisolone if persistent or necrotic; monitor clinically + ESR/CRP + urine/BP (see *Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis*).

**Diagnosis:** **HBV-associated systemic polyarteritis nodosa.**: ACR criteria met: weight loss >4 kg, livedo, myalgia/leg tenderness, neuropathy, diastolic BP >90, raised creatinine (2.7 mg/dL ≈ 239 µmol/L), **HBsAg+** = **7 of 10**; Predictive items: HBsAg+, neuropathy positive; ANCA/cryo/asthma/ENT/GN negative

**Supporting:** nodules along arteries, necrotic ulcers, anaemia, thrombocytosis, leucocytosis. Renal impairment with **hypertension** reflects **renal-artery vasculopathy (renovascular hypertension), not GN**.

**Investigations still needed:** CT/MR or catheter angiography (renal/mesenteric microaneurysms), deep skin/muscle/nerve biopsy, HBeAg/HBV DNA, LFT, nerve conduction studies, urinalysis (bland sediment expected), echo/ECG.
**DDx:** ANCA-associated vasculitis (MPA), cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, SLE vasculitis, infective endocarditis, APS, cholesterol emboli, lymphoma, DADA2.

**Treatment:** **antiviral (entecavir/tenofovir) + short-course steroids + plasma exchange** (avoid prolonged immunosuppression in HBV-PAN); BP control; specialist MDT (rheumatology, hepatology, renal); contact tracing/vaccination (see *Polyarteritis nodosa — systemic, HBV-associated and cutaneous*).

blocks: Diagnosis of PAN; cutaneous vs systemic PAN; causes of livedo and vessel involvement; treatment (see *Polyarteritis nodosa — systemic, HBV-associated and cutaneous* and *Livedo reticularis vs livedo racemosa*).

ul: **QA = 4, Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis):** purpura + arthralgia + abdominal pain + haematuria/proteinuria after a URTI; normal platelets.

**QB = 4, LCV with perivascular IgA and C3 on DIF.**: The course explanation attributes "necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized arteries with negative DIF" to **GPA** as well as PAN. The correct match is: option 1 = **PAN**; option 2 (**small- and medium-vessel vasculitis with necrosis and granulomas**) = **GPA**; option 3 = giant-cell arteritis; option 5 (IgM) = cryoglobulinaemia
**QC = 2, group A β-haemolytic streptococcus.**

**UK additions:** exclude meningococcal sepsis first. The urinalysis already shows blood + protein, so **check BP and the urine protein:creatinine ratio, and discuss with paediatrics** (CKS). Then a structured urine/BP follow-up for ≥6 months.

refer.t: Blood or protein on urine dipstick, or raised BP: same-day discussion with renal or medical team.
Non-blanching rash in an unwell or feverish patient: **suspected meningococcal disease**, 999 (NICE NG240).
Haemoptysis, breathlessness, neuropathy or abdominal pain with purpura: systemic vasculitis, urgent referral.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Blood or protein on urine dipstick, or raised BP: same-day discussion with renal or medical team.
Non-blanching rash in an unwell or feverish patient: **suspected meningococcal disease**, 999 (NICE NG240).
Haemoptysis, breathlessness, neuropathy or abdominal pain with purpura: systemic vasculitis, urgent referral.

**Same day (999/ED):** purpura in an **unwell or febrile** patient — especially a child — **meningococcal sepsis/DIC** (NICE NG240); suspected **endocarditis**; rapidly spreading necrosis; haemoptysis; acute kidney injury; GI bleeding/severe abdominal pain; mononeuritis multiplex.

**Urgent (days):** palpable purpura with **haematuria/proteinuria**, raised creatinine or **hypertension** (renal); systemic symptoms; positive ANCA; nodules/ulcers/livedo racemosa (medium-vessel disease); persistent >4 weeks or recurrent.
**Routine dermatology:** skin-limited, well patient, normal urine/bloods, cause unclear.
Renal failure, pulmonary haemorrhage, neuropathy, gut infarction, ulcers.
Skin-limited forms usually settle; systemic vasculitis needs immunosuppression.

pearls: "**Glass test first.**" Non-blanching + palpable = vasculitis work-up; non-blanching + unwell = 999.
Always **dip the urine** and **check BP** — then repeat at follow-up.
Ask about **every new drug in the last 1–3 weeks**, including OTC ibuprofen and recreational cocaine (levamisole).

blocks.h: Where course teaching differs from UK guidance

head: Topic
Course teaching
UK position (2026)
rows: Course teaching: "necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized arteries with negative DIF" for **GPA** (and PAN)
That option fits **PAN**. GPA = **necrotising small/medium-vessel vasculitis with granulomas** (option 2)
course explanation: monitor urine and BP during active disease

NICE CKS: **exclude meningococcal disease** and leukaemia/ITP first; a **structured urinalysis + BP schedule for ≥6 months**; same-day referral criteria (abdominal, testicular, renal, unwell); paracetamol first, NSAIDs only if no renal involvement
course explanation: ~75% under 8; more severe in adults
Agrees; teach that adults get HSP too (biopsy with DIF — higher nephritis risk)
A student answer: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered over 6 months ± cyclophosphamide for 12 months, after antivirals

For **HBV-associated PAN**: **antivirals + short steroid course + plasma exchange**, avoiding prolonged steroids/cyclophosphamide (HBV flare risk). Long steroid ± cyclophosphamide applies to severe **non-HBV** PAN (ACR/VF 2021; FFS-guided)
A student answer: "high risk of renal involvement"
Correct, but in PAN it is **vascular (renovascular hypertension, infarcts)**; **glomerulonephritis argues against PAN** (a negative predictive item)
Agrees, but the 3-month history does not meet the Schwartz **≥6-month** criterion, and the SLE overlap must be formally assessed; urgent renal referral for the raised creatinine
Agrees; UK practice adds **BP** at the same visit and repeated urinalysis/BP at follow-up
Course teaching: bed rest, hosiery, dapsone
Agrees; dapsone requires **G6PD testing** and FBC/LFT/methaemoglobin monitoring (BNF); check arterial supply before compression
Students: Osler/Janeway "pathognomonic" in some student answers
Not pathognomonic; **Duke–ISCVID 2023** minor criteria; **blood cultures before antibiotics**; NICE CG64: no routine antibiotic prophylaxis
UK: creatinine µmol/L (× 88.4), urea mmol/L (BUN mg/dL × 0.357)

quiz.q: When should you think of Approach to cutaneous vasculitis?
quiz.a: Palpable purpura, haemorrhagic blisters, nodules, livedo or ulcers, especially on the lower legs.
Inflammation of vessel walls from immune complexes, ANCA or infection; small vessels give purpura, medium vessels give nodules, livedo racemosa and ulcers.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Urine dipstick and BP today; FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, ANCA, complement, hepatitis B/C, cryoglobulins as indicated; biopsy within 48 h; stop culprit drugs.
Renal involvement, systemic ANCA vasculitis, endocarditis and meningococcal sepsis.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Blood or protein on urine dipstick, or raised BP: same-day discussion with renal or medical team.
